chapter: Family and early memories of Jelly
title: Jelly's godmother, Catholic upbringing and religion
summary: Talk of his godmother in Watts, her grandmother keeping the girls Catholic, and Jelly's religious advice; she moved to Texas in 1931.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: When I was out there in 1940, and your brother was still living in New York, I'd seen him before, but I went out to see some musicians like Kid Ory and another old-time guitar player, his nickname was Gigi Williams, Norwood Williams. He lived down in Watts. I remember hearing him speak of Gigi. He was running a filling station, and he told me, he said, he thought it was, he said, Jelly Roll's mother. He didn't know it was his godmother. He said, his mother lives over here in Watts. It was his godfather. It was his godmother, and his godmother

died about that time. Yes. That's when he went out. Eddie Hunter and Lolly Hunter. That was his godmother. His godfather. So I didn't get to meet him. But I mean, Lolly was so crazy about my mother that she wanted to take all three of us to register, and my grandmother wanted us to be a red Catholic, see, so she wouldn't let us go. And to what good does it do to hand down religion before a child is old enough to know what they're doing? You know what I mean? I didn't do that with my son. I mean, he, I christened him. I had him christened, and that's all. When he got ready to get married, he went and had to make his communion, be confirmed and everything, because suppose he'd have married a Protestant girl. Then he'd have to change over again, see. Your brother was quite religious,
I think, wasn't he? Yes, he's Catholic. I mean, he's the Catholic, and he was very Catholic, and

that's right. He's quite religious. He would always tell me, baby, take the bitters and the sweets, and remember God's above, and he'll always take care of me. But I mean, I think he admired me, because I never did beg. I never did ask for anything. I couldn't appreciate, couldn't show more appreciations, because I was always thanking him for what he sent, and asked him what I could do for him after I married a doctor. But he said, I'm just so glad you married and doing well. He didn't want anything from me. You went to Texas then, during some of that time, then, when he was— I went to Texas in 1931 and got married, and I came back home in 45 to live. And I—of course, my son finished his—his grammar school and high school worked there, and he went to Texas. He went to Marshall, Texas, to college. My son entered Bishop College, and he graduated from high school in Maine. He went that September to Bishop College and stayed there four years.
